title: Session graduation and demotion strategy to minimize cold-cache penalty for pinned canaries
creator: Ava Martinez
description: Problem: When sessions are pinned to a new model variant during canary rollouts, many of those sessions suffer cold KV-cache and embedding cache misses. This produces a transient latency and cost spike for a subset of users and can bias canary metrics. Goal: Define a session lifecycle (graduation/demotion) and a routing algorithm that smoothly moves sessions between pinned model variants while minimizing cold-cache penalties and preserving canary signal fidelity.
background_and_motivation: Current pin behavior binds session affinity immediately to the target model variant when a pin event occurs (manual pin or canary assignment). For long-lived sessions this causes a front-loaded cost and latency spike as token and prefix caches warm up. That spike skews short-window latency percentiles and can cause premature canary rollbacks. We need a mechanism that staggers or probabilistically transitions sessions to new variants while retaining fast rollback capability and observability.
acceptance_criteria: New session graduation policy is implemented in routing resolver and toggleable via config
Observed 95th latency for pinned-session population reduces by >= 20% during first 30 minutes after a canary assignment versus immediate-hard-pin baseline in benchmark tests
Canary metrics (error rate, latency, quality evals) remain accurate within tolerance; we provide a clear mapping from session cohorts to canary exposure
Rollback to previous variant can happen within 60s for any transitioning cohort and without orphaned affinity state
proposed_solution_overview: Introduce a three-state session lifecycle for pinned canaries: HOLD -> WARMING -> GRADUATED. When a session receives a pin to a canary variant, it enters HOLD (keep routing to previous variant for N requests but mark for progressive transition). A lightweight background sampler nudges a small fraction of requests from HOLD through the canary to populate caches (WARMING). After a TTL or successful warming threshold the session moves to GRADUATED (full routing to canary). Demotion reverses the states in case of rollback. Routing resolver keeps sticky metadata (state, last-warmed-at, warming-attempts) with compact encoding and TTLs to avoid unbounded state.
design_decisions_and_tradeoffs: Use probabilistic warmup (e.g., 5% of requests) vs fixed-count warmup: probabilistic reduces coordination but may take longer to warm heavy sessions
Store minimal state in session-handles (opaque 2-byte flags + epoch counter) to avoid increasing storage pressure in the orchestrator
Warming requests should have priority=low and be subject to capacity controls to avoid overloading canary capacity
Keep rollout observability by tagging warming requests with cohort ids so we can filter metrics; accept some additional metric cardinality
implementation_notes: Routing resolver change: accept 'graduation_policy' with params {hold_requests, warming_fraction, max_warm_attempts, graduation_ttl}
Session handle schema bump: add 8-bit state + 24-bit epoch for rollouts. Backwards compatible default = GRADUATED for existing sessions
KV-cache priming: ensure warming requests pin prefix keys into the canary instance; consider a "fast-path" priming RPC to prefetch hot KV keys for heavy sessions
Capacity gating: integrate with autoscaler signals. If canary GPU utilization > 70% then reduce warming_fraction dynamically
Telemetry: emit events for state transitions and warming attempts with sample keys to help debugging without leaking PII
progress_updates: 2025-02-12: Spike implemented in sandbox routing resolver. Verified local state encoding fits in existing session-handle limit
2025-02-18: Bench harness created to simulate 10k long-lived sessions with realistic prefix distributions; measured cold-cache overhead baseline
2025-02-24: Prototype warming_fraction=0.05 reduced 95th tail by ~18% in synthetic benchmark; observed increased canary GPU load during warm windows
2025-03-02: Incorporated autoscaler gating to reduce warming_fraction when GPU util > 65%; preparing PR for initial review
review_feedback: PM: Ensure product can toggle policy per-customer and exposes canary cohort metrics in Console
Design: Add visualization to rollout timeline showing warmed cohort percentage over time
Security: Confirm telemetry sampling does not include prompt text or user identifiers; OK with cohort-level tags
Infra: State TTLs need to be conservative to avoid sticky misrouting during cross-region migrations
open_questions: What is the correct default hold_requests for interactive vs batch sessions? (5 requests vs 0)
Should warming requests be marked 'non-billable' for customers during canary exposure window? Implications for billing and fairness
Do we need proactive prefetch from control plane vs relying on in-band warming requests for worst-case cold starts?
risk_and_mitigation: Risk: Warming traffic could overload canary under heavy rollouts -> Mitigation: Autoscaler gating + backpressure counters
Risk: Increased metric cardinality -> Mitigation: cohort sampling and aggregated telemetry endpoints
Risk: Sticky state persists during failover causing misrouted sessions -> Mitigation: epoch counter + short TTLs and explicit session invalidate RPC
qa_steps: Deploy feature flag in staging; run bench harness and compare latency tails for immediate-pin vs graduated policy
Simulate rollback during warming window and verify sessions demote to previous variant within 60s
Introduce forced canary overutilization and validate warming_fraction reduces and warming attempts back off
Confirm telemetry shows cohort membership and transition counts; sample traces for 50 warmed sessions
rollback_plan: Feature guarded by runtime flag. Rollback steps: 1) disable graduation policy via flag, 2) invalidate session-state for cohorts by incrementing epoch, 3) drain warming traffic by setting warming_fraction=0, 4) monitor for any lingering affinity and remove stale handles after TTL
